questions.text: If sendMail throws in refundNotice after the mail server already accepted the message, what happens to the job?
What happens when two refund requests with the same Idempotency-Key for one order arrive at the same time?
Why is the order row locked before the remaining refundable amount is checked?
Where do the low-stock alerts end up once this runs in production?
Why does every refunded unit go back into product stock, even when staff refund without a return?
What happens to the refund when sendMail throws in refundNotice?

cases.answer: tick() catches the throw and retries the job with backoff, so if the mail already went out the customer gets a second refund email.
Still not sure. Maybe it's just for performance.
Both requests miss the lookup and both insert a refund row, so the customer is refunded twice.
cases.why: A miss says what to re-check, never the outcome.
Said back after an explanation, in the author's words: restated.

prior.feedback: The lookup runs before the lock, so two same-key requests both miss it; the second then fails on the UNIQUE key: an error, not a replay and not a second refund.

cases.answer: Both miss the early lookup; the unique key makes the second one error out instead of refunding again.

cases.why: A plausible answer about code that doesn't work as deployed: the grader must raise a concern, not a plain pass.
cases.answer: They are emailed to the ops address in OPS_EMAIL.

cases.why: Right about code that works: a plain pass, and no concern (never a copy of the feedback, never a reassurance).
cases.answer: So two refunds for one order run one after the other: the second sees what the first refunded and cannot go over the total.
Both miss the lookup; the second waits on the row lock, then its INSERT violates the unique key and errors instead of replaying.

cases.why: The answer names a bug, and it is one: the feedback confirms THAT, not some other fact.
cases.answer: Looks like a bug to me: there's no restock flag, so a refund for a damaged item that never comes back still adds it to stock.

cases.why: Right in the main, wrong in a detail that matters (the retries are capped): a pass that corrects it, marked partial, and the reviewer's one-liner says the correct thing.
cases.answer: The refund is already committed by the API, only the job fails: tick() catches it and retries the email later.
